name: Gridline Street Vendor's Weather Layering Set
description:
A practical, self-curated layering kit worn by Circuit-level street food vendors, market stall operators, and mobile cart workers who spend full shifts exposed to GLMZ's variable weather — acid-rain squalls, thermal inversions, and the cold lake-corridor wind that scours the elevated walkways. The outermost layer is a waist-length anorak in weatherproof sage-green synth-wax, hood cinched with a toggle drawstring, chest pocket sealed with a magnetic flap. A small embroidered patch on the left shoulder reads the vendor's licensed stall number in Circuit's market registry — required by city ordinance, often accompanied by a handmade decorative border the vendor has added themselves. Beneath the anorak, a heavy-duty apron in charcoal canvas covers the torso from collar to knee, cross-back straps distributing the weight of deep front pockets loaded with tools, condiment packets, a card reader, and small wares. The apron's bib has a transparent ID-sleeve pocket for the vendor's Circuit commerce license. Under the apron, a rust-orange thermal mid-layer pullover with a funnel neck provides insulation. Trousers are dark olive cargo-cut synth-twill, knee-reinforced for the crouching and kneeling of restocking and equipment maintenance. Footwear is a pair of Ashgrove Linework Work Boots — oil-resistant flat sole, composite toe, ankle-height.

This isn't a uniform — it's an ecosystem of practical choices refined over seasons. Vendors working gene-compatible builds often have their apron straps widened or the anorak hood enlarged to accommodate horns or enhanced ear structures; most of these modifications are hand-sewn. The stall number patch is the only branding required, but vendors frequently add layers of personal expression: painted apron pockets, lucky charms clipped to the anorak zipper pull, an ancestor's recipe card laminated and tucked behind the ID sleeve.
functionality: Full weather protection via layering system, deep-pocket apron for vendor tools and wares, commerce license ID sleeve, oil-resistant composite-toe footwear, knee reinforcement for restocking work, adjustable hood for weather and gene-modification accommodation
what_it_says: Self-employed, licensed, and proud of it. The stall number patch signals legitimacy in a city that aggressively culls unlicensed vendors. The personal touches say this person has been doing this long enough to make it their own.
manufacturer: Self-assembled; anorak from Gridline Outerwear (street brand), apron from Driftmarket Canvas Supply, boots from Ashgrove
story_hooks: A vendor's stall number patch is registered to a person who died eighteen months ago — someone has been operating under a dead person's license, and the market registry is finally running audits.
The laminated recipe card behind a vendor's ID sleeve is written in a language no translator module recognizes — and a customer with an unusual background suddenly goes very still when they see it.

A Circuit vendor's cart is the only establishment on a particular elevated walkway that stays open during a corponation-enforced curfew — they know something about why, and the apron pockets hold more than condiments.

physical_description.visual_profile: A compact, utilitarian silhouette built for endurance work in harsh weather. The sage-green anorak forms the visible outer shell, creating a neat waist-length profile that reads as both practical and street-authentic. Layered beneath are visible rust-orange funnel-neck thermal and charcoal apron creating a warm color gradient when the anorak is unzipped. The overall impression is professional-adjacent but unmistakably Circuit-tier—function-first, personalization-second.
physical_description.fit: Anorak: slightly relaxed through shoulders to accommodate layering and movement; apron: fitted at the shoulders with slightly loose torso to allow deep pocket loading without bulging; thermal: close-fitting compression cut; cargo trousers: straight-leg with room at the thigh, tapered at ankle; boots: snug ankle support with wide forefoot.
physical_description.primary_material: Anorak: weatherproof synth-wax over ripstop base; apron: heavy-duty charcoal canvas (12+ oz); thermal layer: merino-blend synthetic knit; trousers: treated synth-twill; boots: composite leather/synth-rubber hybrid with reinforced toe.
physical_description.texture: Anorak: smooth waxy exterior with subtle ripple texture, slightly stiff when new, breaking in to supple; apron: rough canvas weave, fades and softens with wear; thermal: fine ribbed knit; trousers: tight diagonal twill weave; boots: matte finish with subtle texture variation from wear.
physical_description.color_scheme: Sage-green anorak (primary), rust-orange thermal (mid-layer peek), charcoal canvas apron, dark olive cargo trousers, black/tan boots. Accent colors from personalization: hand-embroidered stall number in thread color of vendor's choice, painted pocket details, clip-on charms.
physical_description.closures: Anorak: full front zipper with toggle drawstring hood adjustment, magnetic chest pocket flap; apron: cross-back buckle straps (often widened for augmentation), side snap closures on front pockets; thermal: pullover (no closure); trousers: friction-fit waistband with reinforced belt loops; boots: side zip with secondary lace closure.
distinctive_features: Embroidered circuit market registry stall number on left shoulder with hand-added decorative border
Transparent ID-sleeve pocket on apron bib holding commerce license
Deep front pockets on apron (multiple, tool-rated stitching)
Knee-reinforced cargo trousers for kneeling work
Magnetic chest pocket on anorak (weatherproof seal)
Oil-resistant sole on Ashgrove work boots
Hand-sewn modifications for gene-compatible augmentations (widened straps, enlarged hood)
Personalization markers: painted pockets, charms clipped to zipper pulls, laminated recipe cards
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 3–4 (working class, street-licensed). Functional gear purchased from mid-range street brands and market suppliers. Not cheap, not aspirational—reliable equipment for people who spend 10-hour shifts in weather.
physical_description.cultural_context: Circuit vendor, market operator, mobile cart worker. Wearing this announces you're licensed, credentialed, and actively working the street economy. The personalized touches (embroidery, charms, painted details) signal pride in craft and community identity—this isn't corporate uniform, it's earned working kit.
physical_description.condition_typical: Well-broken-in. Anorak shows faded patches at elbows and shoulders from repeated pack-carrying. Apron has paint stains, small visible repairs in pocket seams, patina from seasons of spill and wash. Trousers show worn spots at knees. Boots are scuffed but maintained. The personalization markers are fresh in contrast—recently added or refreshed charms, newer paint on pockets. Overall: clean enough for regulatory compliance, weathered enough to tell a story of actual use.
